title: What questions should you ask at the end of a consulting interview?
description: Good and bad questions to ask your interviewer at the end of a consulting interview, with examples that show curiosity and research.
hook: At the end of a consulting interview, ask one or two specific questions about the interviewer's own experience and work, ideally building on something they said earlier, rather than generic questions you could answer from the firm's website. "Do you have any questions for me?" is not a formality. It is your last chance to show curiosity and leave a good impression, and a genuine chance to learn whether you want to work there.
body:
What this moment is for

Firms expect you to ask. McKinsey's interviewing page tells candidates to bring questions, and BCG's interview process page describes the questions you ask at the end as a way to understand whether you are a fit. A good question does three things: it shows you were listening, it shows how you think, and it gets you information you can use, including in your next "Why this firm?" answer.

Weak questions

What is the culture like?
How many hours do you work?

Why they fall short: the first is so broad it invites a generic answer. The second may be a fair concern, but framed this way to an interviewer it can sound as if workload is your main worry. Both miss the chance to have a real conversation.

Strong questions

These are examples, not a script. Adapt them to the person and what they have told you.

About their experience

You mentioned you moved from the healthcare practice into private equity work. What made you switch, and how did the firm help you make that move?
What's something you've learned on your current project that surprised you?

About how the work really happens

On the last project you enjoyed, what made the team effective when the problem was still unclear?
How does your team know a recommendation has actually changed what a client does, six months later?

About joining and growing

Which skills do people joining from industry tend to underestimate in their first year?

Why they work: they are personal, specific to the interviewer, and invite a story rather than a brochure answer. A question that builds on something they said earlier is the strongest of all, because it proves you were listening.

Match the question to the person

InterviewerBest placed to talk about
Consultant or managerDay-to-day work, feedback, team dynamics, their projects
PartnerHow client needs are changing, how the office builds new capabilities
RecruiterProcess, timelines, training, logistics and policies

Respect what each person can know. A first-year consultant cannot tell you the firm's strategy for the next decade, and a partner is not the right person to ask about the recruiting timeline.

Listen and follow up

Ask one question, then actually listen. If the answer is interesting, ask a follow-up: "What did that look like in practice?" A two-minute conversation about a real project is more memorable than firing off five polished questions from a list. Prepare three or four in advance so you have options, but expect to use only one or two.

If you do want to know about hours, workload or flexibility, you can ask in a way that invites a real answer: "How do teams on your projects manage busy periods?" Questions about policies are best put to the recruiter, and anything already on the careers page should only come up if you are asking how it works in practice.

Common mistakes

  • Saying "No, I think you've covered everything." It suggests a lack of curiosity. Always have at least one question.
  • Asking what you could have looked up. "Which industries do you work in?" shows you have not done your homework.
  • Reading from a list. It feels mechanical. Pick the question that fits the conversation you just had.
  • Asking about the outcome. "How did I do?" puts the interviewer in an awkward position. Save feedback requests for the recruiter after the decision.
  • Running over time. If the interviewer is short of time, ask one question and thank them.

Try it now

1. Improve: "What do you like about working here?"

Show the answer

Make it specific to them: "You said your last project was in retail. What was the moment on that project when you felt the work really made a difference for the client?"

2. Your interviewer is a partner and you have five minutes. Which question fits better: "How long does training last?" or "How are clients' needs changing in your sector?"

Show the answer

The second. A partner sees the market and client relationships; training details are better asked of a recruiter.

3. Write three questions for your next interview: one about the interviewer's experience, one about how the work happens, one about growing in the role.

Show the answer

Check each one: could you answer it from the website? If yes, rewrite it. Does it invite a story? If it can be answered with a number or a yes, rewrite it.

Where to practise next

The best questions come from earlier conversations with people at the firm, so read networking for consulting. What you learn will also strengthen your "Why this firm?" answer. For a realistic picture of the job to base questions on, see what consultants do all day.
